archetype.name: Dual-Threat (efficiency-first passer)
archetype.definition: A quarterback whose passing now carries the offense on modest volume, with scrambles and designed runs as a second engine rather than the main one.

report.headline: Best-in-league efficiency on a soft slate, now paused by a sprained ankle.
report.take:
Through four starts Jackson has been the most efficient passer in football by the broadest measure. His 10.74 adjusted net yards per dropback ranks first of 45 qualifiers, his 0.363 EPA per dropback ranks third, and his 8.29 CPOE ranks second. What makes it unusual is the shape: he throws only 24 times a game in an offense that passes less than situation predicts (-4.7 pass rate over expected, 26th). So his yardage (241.8 a game, 15th) looks ordinary while every throw is worth far more than average. He is not piling up attempts. He is making the few he gets count.

The driver is accuracy, and that is the real change. His completion rate is up 7.2 points on last year and his CPOE is up 6.5. Across his career only 2019 and 2024 came close to this kind of on-target play, and he has never sustained a CPOE near +8. The production is spread across depths. Short throws return 0.504 EPA, intermediate 0.904 and deep 0.745, and Zay Flowers has turned 19 targets into 27.7 EPA at 1.46 a target, more than any other target. The legs are back as a supplement too. He is rushing for 36 yards a game (5th) after 26.8 last year, and his 10 scrambles have produced six first downs.

The schedule is the caveat. The four defenses he faced rank 24th, 27th, 31st and 22nd in defensive EPA today, so none of this has been tested against a good unit. There are leaks underneath the gloss. Third down is flat (0.01 EPA, 34.8% conversions, though with 9.2 yards to go on average). He has been below average in the red zone (-0.07 EPA, -7 CPOE) even with four touchdowns there. His 29.2% pressure-to-sack rate is a lifelong trait that comes with how long he holds the ball. He also ranks 32nd of 37 in bad-throw rate, which sits oddly beside the elite CPOE: the misses are there, but the completions he does make are harder than expected.

Now he is hurt. He played only 52% of snaps in Week 4 and sat out Weeks 5 and 6 with an ankle sprain while Tyler Huntley started, including a 13-10 loss to Cleveland. The coach calls him day-to-day with a chance to practice this week. When he returns, expect the passing efficiency to come down toward very good rather than historic as the defenses get better. Expect the rushing to be the first thing the ankle takes away.

strengths.title: Accuracy jump fuels every depth
strengths.body: His CPOE is second among qualifiers and up sharply from last season, and it shows at every depth rather than in one hot zone. Intermediate throws (15 attempts) and deep shots (18) have been worth enormous EPA, while the short game is efficient enough to carry drives. Some of this will regress against better defenses because no season of his has held a CPOE this high. His 2019 and 2024 seasons show the ceiling is real.

strengths.title: Explosive connection with Flowers
strengths.body: Zay Flowers has been the big-play outlet, producing far more EPA per target than anyone else in the offense. Mark Andrews draws the most targets but at a modest rate. Flowers is where the chunk plays come from, and that chemistry is durable as long as both are healthy. The per-target figure is on 19 targets and will cool, but the role is stable.

strengths.title: Legs as a drive extender
strengths.body: His rushing is back near his usual level after a down 2025. Scrambles are paying off at 0.48 EPA apiece, and six of the 10 moved the chains, so the time he spends holding the ball buys real value. How much of this survives an ankle sprain is the open question for the next few weeks.

concerns.title: Ankle sprain clouds availability and mobility
concerns.body: He is listed Out, has missed two games, and is described as day-to-day with a possible return to practice. Even if he plays, a sprained ankle threatens the scrambling and the off-platform creation that turn his long time to throw into gains instead of sacks. This is the biggest variable in his outlook.

concerns.title: Untested against real defenses
concerns.body: Every defense he has faced ranks 22nd or worse in defensive EPA today, including the 31st-ranked Cowboys in his best EPA game. The efficiency is genuine, but its level was set against soft opposition. A step down is likely once the schedule stiffens.

concerns.title: Sacks and money-down leaks
concerns.body: A pressure-to-sack rate near 30% is who he has always been; last season's was worse. It comes with how long he holds the ball, and the scrambles mostly pay for it. The bigger issues are third down and the red zone, where his efficiency disappears. Both are small samples (23 and 15 plays), so they are more likely noise than a flaw, but they are worth watching.

trend.note: Three of his four games landed between 10 and 12 passing EPA, with a dip to 3.3 in the Week 2 loss to New Orleans. The run stopped when the ankle cut his Week 4 to half the snaps and kept him out of Weeks 5 and 6.

nextGame.headline: If he plays: a leaky short defense with a dangerous pass rush
nextGame.body:
Cincinnati's defense is built in a way that cuts both ways for him. It is 29th against short passes, which is where most of his attempts and touchdowns come from, and it gives up a lot of yardage to quarterbacks (26th). Tight ends feast on it, and it is 28th against the run. But it is 5th against deep passes, which takes away some of the chunk plays Flowers has produced, and its sack rate is 3rd in the league. The Bengals' offense passes more than anyone over expected, and the total sits at 51.5 with Baltimore -2.5. That points to a game where the Ravens may have to throw more than their usual 24 times.

Availability decides everything here. Jackson himself is the headline: day-to-day, possibly practicing, and listed Out as of Monday. Center Cam Jurgens, a 100% snap starter, is out with a concussion, which weakens the middle of the line against that pass rush. Rashod Bateman left the Browns game with a shoulder injury but "should be OK." Tight end Matt Hibner is out, which concentrates more of the tight-end work on Andrews. On Cincinnati's side, nothing on the injury report meaningfully touches the matchup.

keyMatchups.title: Bengals pass rush vs no Jurgens
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati gets home at one of the league's highest rates, and Baltimore is missing its starting center. Pair that with Jackson's career-long tendency to take sacks when pressured and a possibly limited ankle, and drive-killing sacks are the main threat. Quick throws underneath are the counter.

keyMatchups.title: Short game into a soft underbelly
keyMatchups.body: His short passing has been highly efficient, and Cincinnati is among the worst defenses against short throws. That is the path to efficiency even if the deep shots dry up against a top-five deep defense.

keyMatchups.title: Andrews against a TE-friendly defense
keyMatchups.body: Opposing lead tight ends score well above their usual output against Cincinnati, and tight ends draw an outsized share of targets against it. With Hibner out, Andrews should soak up those looks. He is Jackson's most-targeted option already.

nextGame.watch: Whether Jackson practices fully this week, and if he plays, whether he still scrambles freely or stays in the pocket on a sore ankle.

restOfSeason.body:
The accuracy gains look partly real: completion rate and CPOE are up across every depth, not just one lucky zone. But a +8 CPOE and 10-plus adjusted yards per dropback built against four bottom-tier defenses will not hold. Expect him to settle at very good efficiency, roughly 0.18 to 0.28 EPA per dropback, which is still well above the league's 0.034. Volume stays modest because Baltimore runs more than situations dictate, so passing yards should sit around 205-245 a game unless shootouts force more attempts. The touchdown rate should hold near the low-to-mid 1s a game, and the red-zone inefficiency likely evens out.

The rushing is the piece most at risk. An ankle sprain in a 29-year-old who has played through injury-shortened seasons before argues for fewer designed runs and more caution early, so his rushing likely starts near the low end and climbs if the ankle cooperates. The sack rate is a career trait and will stay roughly where it is, worse behind a line missing Jurgens.
swingFactors: How the ankle affects his scrambling
Whether Baltimore's pass rate rises in shootouts

confidence.note: Four games, all against weak defenses, and an active ankle injury with an uncertain return.
